solution:
The correct option is **(i) 1**.

Rewritten statement: **The number of electrons in the outermost shell of alkali metals is 1.**

The chapter identifies group 1 as "the family of alkali metals" and states that "the number of valence electrons in all these elements from the group 1, that is, the family of alkali metals, is the same". Table 2.8 prints their configurations — Li 2,1 · Na 2,8,1 · K 2,8,8,1 — with one electron in the outermost shell in every case. Two valence electrons would make them the alkaline earth metals of group 2, and seven would make them the halogens of group 17.

solution:
The correct option is **(i) Group 2**.

Rewritten statement: **Alkaline earth metals have valency 2. This means that their position in the modern periodic table is in Group 2.**

The chapter states that "the valency of an element is determined by the number of electrons present in the outermost shell of its atoms", so a valency of 2 means two valence electrons; and it names that group directly: "the elements beryllium (Be), magnesium (Mg) and calcium (Ca) belong to the group 2, that is, the family of alkaline earth metals. There are two electrons in their outermost shell." Group 16 is ruled out because its elements have six valence electrons; Period 2 is a horizontal row and does not fix a valency at all; and group 2 lies in the s-block, since the chapter says "The s-block contains the groups 1 and 2", not the d-block.

solution:
The correct option is **(i) Na**.

Rewritten statement: *Molecular formula of the chloride of an element X is XCl. This compound is a solid having high melting point. Sodium (Na) would be present in the same group as X.*

In \(\mathrm{XCl}\) one atom of X combines with one atom of chlorine, so the valency of X is 1 and X has one electron in its outermost shell. The chapter states that the number of valence electrons is the same for every element of a group, so X belongs to group 1 — "the family of alkali metals". Of the four options only sodium is a group 1 element: table 2.8 gives Na = 2,8,1. That the compound is a solid of high melting point fits an ionic chloride of a metal, and the chapter's table 2.5 lists NaCl among the compounds of sodium.

The others do not fit: magnesium (2,8,2), aluminium (2,8,3) and silicon (2,8,4) have two, three and four valence electrons, so their chlorides would be \(\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{SiCl_{4}}\), not \(\mathrm{XCl}\).

solution:
The correct option is **(ii) p-block**.

Rewritten statement: **The nonmetals of the modern periodic table are found in the p-block.**

The chapter states that "The groups 13 to 18 constitute the p-block", and that "A zig-zag line can be drawn in the p-block of the periodic table... All the metals lie on the left side of the zig-zag line while all the nonmetals lie on the right side. The metalloid elements lie along the border of this zig-zag line." Since that dividing line lies inside the p-block, the nonmetals lie in the p-block.

The other blocks do not hold them: "The s-block contains the groups 1 and 2" — the alkali and alkaline earth metals; "The groups 3 to 12 constitute the d-block", whose elements "are called transition elements"; and "the lanthanide and actinide series at the bottom form the f-block".

(The chapter notes separately that "the ambiguity about the position of hydrogen is not removed even in the modern periodic table" — hydrogen is shown in group 1, in the s-block.)
